NAEB Cross-Reference Digest Dashboard

Purpose: turn the cross-referenced plant-use spreadsheet into a readable public-facing dashboard. Think of each row as a museum note: “Someone historically recorded this plant being used this way.” It is not a recipe, prescription, recommendation, or proof of current cultural practice.

Data source: Native American Ethnobotany Database / BRIT Cross-reference file: Generated:
Public disclaimer: These are historical ethnobotanical records. Medicinal or “Drug” records are not medical advice. Do not use this dashboard to diagnose, treat, dose, harvest, sell, or recommend plant medicines. Keep the original tribe label, source, page number, and citation attached to records. Safer wording: “Historically recorded as used by [tribe label] for [use category/use note].”

What this dashboard says, in plain words

1. Pick a plant

Search a scientific or common name. The dashboard shows the historical use categories attached to that plant.

2. Read the source line

Every detailed record keeps the original tribe label and citation where the workbook had it.

3. Use careful wording

Say “historically recorded as used,” not “this plant cures.”

Plant Explorer

Search plants from your master plant list. Click a plant card to open a digest with category counts, readable summaries, record examples, and citations.

Record Browser

This is the safest place to cite individual records because it shows plant, tribe label, use note, page, and citation together.

Sources & Citations

Use this section when the dashboard will be shared online. It lists grouped citation text, counts, plants, tribe labels, and source URLs where present.

No-Match Review

These are plants from your list that did not match NAEB by the scientific-name binomial used in the workbook. A no-match does not prove the plant has no ethnobotanical records; it may be absent from this scrape, listed under a synonym, or spelled differently.

How to read this

Small-child version

A plant can have many old notes. Each note says: a group name, a plant name, what someone wrote that people used it for, and where that note came from. We keep the note and the book/page together so people can check it.

Best public wording

“Historically recorded as used by [tribe label] for [use category/use note].”

Wording to avoid

Do not say “This plant cures...,” “Native Americans used this for...,” or wording that makes broad claims without tribe label, source, and citation.

Important limitations

Original source labels may be historic, broad, inconsistent, or outdated. This dashboard is a cross-reference subset of the plant master list, not a complete cultural or botanical authority.
